notes.meaning: Agur son of Jakeh introduces his wise words, sharing an inspired message with his friends Ithiel and Ucal. Although the Bible tells us nothing else about Agur's life, his sayings were preserved by God as holy Scripture. His opening words show an honest teacher speaking God's truth to others.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern translators divide the Hebrew letters differently to read the names Ithiel and Ucal as a statement of weariness: 'I am weary, O God, and worn out.'

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translation treats the names as ordinary descriptive words, translating them as 'The words of the gatherer, the son of the vomiter.'

notes.meaning: Agur humbly admits that he has no natural wisdom and feels far less knowledgeable than other people. He knows that human cleverness cannot figure out the Holy One on its own. Recognizing our own limits and lack of understanding is the first step toward genuine wisdom.

Agur asks who has ever climbed up to heaven, gathered the wind in their fists, or wrapped the ocean waters in a garment. No human being has ever done these things; only the Creator governs the entire universe. The questions show that God's ways and his family are far beyond human discovery.

differ.view: The question about the Son points to a distinct divine person who shares God's nature and has existed with the Father from eternity.
The verse exalts God's incomprehensible greatness, but Christians should be cautious about resting the doctrine of the Trinity on such an obscure poetic passage.
The verse prophetically points to Christ, who came down from heaven to save us and ascended to heaven to be our advocate.

notes.meaning: Every single word from God is pure and reliable, like precious metal refined in a furnace without any dirt or flaw. God also acts as a protective shield for all who seek safety in him. We can trust his promises completely because they never fail.

Agur warns against adding human rules, ideas, or traditions to God's inspired words. Trying to improve on God's message brings his rebuke and exposes the person as a liar. God's truth is already complete and must not be altered by human opinions.

Agur asks God for two specific blessings before he dies: to keep him far from falsehood, and to grant him a modest life between poverty and riches. He asks for only his daily portion of food, rather than luxury. He worries that having too much might make him proud and forgetful of God, while being desperately poor might tempt him to steal and bring shame on God's name.

A person should never slander or bring petty complaints against a servant to their master. Servants already occupy a difficult and vulnerable position in life. If you mistreat them without cause, God hears their grievance and will hold you guilty.

Agur describes an ungodly group of people who show utter disrespect toward their parents. Instead of honoring their father and mother, they curse them and refuse to speak well of them. Breaking the command to honor parents reveals a deeply rebellious heart.

Another group considers themselves clean and upright in their own estimation. In reality, their hearts are still stained and unwashed from the filth of their sins. Thinking you are morally perfect blinds you to your real need for God's mercy.

A third group is ruined by haughtiness and overwhelming pride. They carry themselves with lifted eyelids and look down on others with disdain. Arrogance in the eyes shows a heart full of self-importance.

A fourth group acts with savage cruelty toward those who are defenseless. Their sharp words and greedy actions are like swords and knives that devour the needy. They use their power to crush people who cannot fight back.

The blood-sucking leech is pictured as constantly crying out for more, driven by endless appetite. Agur compares this greed to four things that never say they have enough: the grave that swallows the dead, a barren womb yearning for children, dry earth drinking up water, and a fire that burns up everything in its path. These images warn us that unchecked greed is never satisfied.

A child who mocks their father or sneers at their mother's instruction faces a tragic end. In the ancient world, an unburied body left in a valley became food for ravens and vultures. Scorn toward parents leads to self-destruction and ruin.

Agur marvels at four things whose hidden paths cannot be traced by the eye. An eagle soars through the sky without leaving a trail, a snake glides over a smooth rock without footsteps, a ship sails the deep ocean and leaves no lasting track, and a young man wins the love of a maiden. God has filled creation with mysteries that stir human wonder.

An unfaithful woman acts as if her sin leaves no mark at all. She commits adultery as casually as eating a meal, cleans her face, and claims she has done nothing wrong. A hardened conscience can make a person completely blind to their own wickedness.

Society is turned upside down when unsuited people gain authority and mistreat others. Agur lists four intolerable situations: a servant who becomes an arrogant king, a reckless fool who prospers with plenty of food, a bitter and unloved woman who gets married and vents her anger, and a servant girl who replaces her mistress. When pride and sudden power meet, everyone around them suffers.

Agur points out four creatures on the earth that are tiny in size yet exceptionally wise. God gave these small animals remarkable instincts to help them survive and thrive. Real strength comes from God-given wisdom rather than physical bulk.

Ants are physically weak insects, yet they show immense wisdom by gathering and storing food throughout the summer. They work hard while the weather is favorable so they will survive the cold months. Their discipline teaches us to prepare wisely for the future.

Rock badgers, or coneys, are small, defenseless animals, yet they make their shelters high up in rocky cliffs. They know their physical weakness and find safety in the strong rock. We can learn to hide ourselves in the Lord when we feel helpless.

Locusts have no commander or king to lead them, yet they fly and march together in perfectly organized swarms. Their teamwork and unity allow them to accomplish what one alone could never do. God's people can achieve great things when they work together peacefully.

A small lizard can easily be caught in a human hand, yet its quiet skill and persistence allow it to live even inside royal palaces. Its humble size does not stop it from entering grand places. Diligence and patience can open doors that raw force cannot open.

Agur lists four examples of beings that walk with great dignity and fearless strength. A lion strides forward boldly and never retreats before any beast, a rooster or hunting dog steps out with confidence, a male goat leads the flock with poise, and a king marches with his army without fear of rebellion. These creatures show the majesty and courage God has built into his world.

If you have acted foolishly by boasting of yourself, or if you have begun scheming to do wrong, stop right away and put your hand over your mouth. Catching your pride early keeps words from turning into open rebellion and hurt. Keeping silent and admitting an error prevents further sin.

Just as churning milk produces butter and hitting a nose makes it bleed, stirring up anger inevitably creates fights. Actions produce natural and predictable results, so provoking someone will always ignite conflict. Wise people calm heated tempers before words turn into bitter quarrels.
